To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a hardware Gaussian noise generator is capable of generating a Gaussian noise sequence that accurately models the PDF, at very low BERs (10/sup -8/ to 10/ sup -9/), and at a very high clock frequency of 133 MHz.
the hardware Gaussian noise generator can run at speeds up to seven times faster than the fastest PC and can run at speeds that are up to 50 times faster with parallelization.
the Gaussian noise generator is capable of generating 50 million samples per second on a 105 MHz FPGA, and the performance degrades with the increase in number of parallel instances.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a hardware Gaussian noise generator for use in hardware simulations of digital communication systems.
a novel hardware implementation of Gaussian noise generation for hardware-based simulations of channel coding algorithms.
1) the design of a high-speed, high-precision Gaussian noise generator, 2) its application to a hardware simulator for LDPC codes, and 3) the exploration of its performance and limitations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed noise generator has the potential to improve simulation speed by orders of magnitudes.
the hardware implementation of Gaussian noise generator is a promising approach to improve the speed of hardware simulation of digital communication systems.
the hardware-based noise generator is a promising approach for improving code evaluation speed, but it has not yet reached its full potential. (Abstract shortened by UMI.)
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Gaussian noise generator has a good tradeoff between accuracy and speed.
we have designed a noise generator that is fast and accurate, and that it is possible to achieve a speedup of several orders of magnitude over software simulation.
the hardware-based Gaussian noise generators are able to run at a much higher clock speed than their software counterparts, and are therefore capable of running at much higher BERs than the latter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Gaussian noise generator can be designed and implemented in hardware for high-speed simulation of channel codes.
the design of a noise generator for low BER simulations is not trivial.
a high-performance noise generator for hardware simulation is feasible.
